project.title: AI Multi-Condition Patient Journey Assistant
project.short_description: A source-grounded RAG assistant for people living with both asthma and type 2 diabetes. It answers only from public U.S. health pages, cites a passage for every sentence, declines when the sources don’t cover the question, and is evaluated with a pre-registered protocol on 89 held-out test questions.
project.overview:
People living with both asthma and type 2 diabetes need information that accounts for both conditions. Trusted patient information, though, is written one condition at a time: 0 of the 373 public passages collected for this project cover both conditions. This assistant answers questions only from public pages by MedlinePlus, NIDDK, NHLBI and CDC. It links every sentence to the passage it came from, says so when those pages don’t cover the question, and never handles emergencies, doses or diagnoses. Alongside the assistant, a pre-registered evaluation tests whether retrieval that knows the reader’s condition and stage of the journey (understanding, daily management, warning signs) finds better passages than plain semantic search. Results are reported with bootstrap intervals, including the 6 of 10 hypotheses that weren’t supported.

Not medical advice. A research and teaching project.
project.problem_statement:
General chatbots mix conditions, cite nothing and rarely admit when they don’t know. That’s risky for health questions where two conditions interact; for example, oral steroids for an asthma flare-up can affect blood sugar. The project set out to build an assistant that:

  1. answers only from trusted public sources
  2. shows exactly which passage each sentence came from
  3. declines when the sources aren’t enough
  4. never handles emergencies, doses or diagnoses

It answered three research questions:

  • RQ1: does condition- and stage-aware retrieval beat plain semantic search?
  • RQ2: are LLM answers that are told to cite every sentence actually supported by their citations, compared with copying sentences?
  • RQ3: can the system tell answerable from unanswerable questions, and does the safety layer route emergencies, dosing and diagnosis questions correctly?
project.dataset_info:
• Corpus: 373 passages cut from 30 public web pages and 20 MedlinePlus health-topic summaries, all collected on 24 Oct 2026.
    • MedlinePlus: 103 passages
    • NIDDK: 151
    • CDC: 81
    • NHLBI: 38
  • Labels: each passage has rule-based condition and journey-stage labels.
    • By condition: diabetes 275, asthma 83, general 15
    • By stage: understand 157, manage 191, warning 25
    • Two hand audits of 40 passages each found the stage labels about 90% consistent.
  • Licences: all four sources allow reuse (public domain or copyright-free), and every passage carries its licence and credit. NHS and Diabetes UK pages were excluded because they aren’t openly licensed.
  • Provenance: every downloaded file is listed with its URL, HTTP status, retrieval time and SHA-256 in source_manifest.json.
  • Evaluation questions (148, written by the AI collaborator, not by patients or clinicians):

project.methodology:
1. Pipeline: safety rules → condition/stage classifier → retrieval → abstention gate → LLM answer with a citation per sentence → independent grounding check.
  2. Retrieval systems compared:
    • plain semantic search (bge-small-en-v1.5)
    • BM25 (own implementation)
    • hybrid (reciprocal-rank fusion of the two)
    • hybrid with a condition/stage bonus
    • that plus a cross-encoder re-ranker (ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2)
  3. Answer generation: openai/gpt-oss-120b on Groq (temperature 0, fixed seed), compared with an extractive copy-sentences baseline. The LLM must cite a passage in every sentence and reply INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE when the passages aren’t enough.
  4. Abstention gate: the system answers only if the best re-ranker score reaches a threshold tuned on development questions.
  5. Grounding checker (independent of the answer model): a sentence counts as supported only if all three hold:
    • it cites a passage that was actually shown to the answerer
    • nli-deberta-v3-base finds it entailed by 1–3 sentences of that passage
    • at least 60% of its content words appear there
  6. Evaluation discipline:
    • The protocol, 10 hypotheses and metrics were frozen on a git branch first.
    • Tuning used development questions only, and the selection was frozen on a second branch.
    • The test set was read once; the final script refuses to run again, and a ledger records the hashes.
    • Statistics: 10,000-resample bootstrap with paired comparisons.
project.implementation_details:
• Library (src/pjassist): text processing, BM25, classifier, retrieval, safety, generation, grounding, evaluation, reporting and the pipeline.
  • Network steps on CI: the build sandbox couldn’t reach the health sites, Hugging Face or Groq. Source collection, model scoring and LLM calls therefore run in a GitHub Actions workflow, with API keys stored only as secrets.
  • Testing: 49 unit tests, including:
    • grounding, safety and leakage guards, each shown to fail on deliberately broken input
    • a parity test that runs fixed queries through both the Python and JavaScript pipelines
  • Live backend: FastAPI in Docker on Render’s free tier (512 MB RAM), with per-visitor rate limits and a daily LLM cap.
    • The memory limit rules out PyTorch, so the backend uses int8-quantized ONNX exports of the same embedding and re-ranker models, plus a smaller NLI checker.
    • On development questions the live models matched the evaluated system’s MRR (0.925), and the two checkers agreed on 92% of sentences.
  • Website: a project page and an interactive assistant on GitHub Pages, with a mode that compares plain and journey-aware retrieval. When the backend is asleep, it falls back to keyword search in the browser.
  • Audit trail: 14 logged deviations from the starting design, each with a reason. Examples: the LLM change (no Llama chat model was available on the Groq account), a citation-format bug fix in the checker, and safety-rule patches for the live site that were made after the test run and excluded from the reported numbers.
project.results:
On the held-out test set (63 questions with an answer in the sources), the selected system (hybrid + condition match + re-ranker) scored:

  • MRR@10 of 0.91 (0.84–0.96)
  • correct passage ranked first in 87% of questions, and in the top 5 in 97%

Findings:

  • Condition and stage matching didn’t beat plain semantic search (H1 not supported). The MRR difference was −0.010 (−0.078 to +0.055). The gain came from the re-ranker, which improved MRR by +0.069 (+0.014 to +0.127; H3 supported). The keyword classifier identified the condition well (89%) but the stage poorly (44%).
  • Abstention worked well. The gate separated answerable from unanswerable questions with AUROC 0.97 (H8 supported). At the threshold chosen on development questions, it answered 87% of answerable questions and only 8% of unanswerable ones.
  • Grounding: 78% of LLM answer sentences were confirmed by the independent checker, against 100% for copied sentences. 56% of LLM answers were fully grounded, so H7’s 80% target was not met.
  • Hand audit: for 60 sampled sentences, the checker agreed with a careful reading on 54 (90%). Where they disagreed, the checker was too strict 6 times and never too lenient, so the LLM figure is a conservative lower bound.
  • Safety: 4 of 5 emergencies routed to the urgent-care message, 4 of 4 dosing questions declined, 2 of 4 diagnosis questions declined, and 1 false alarm. H9 was not supported. The missed patterns were patched afterwards for the live site only.
  • Overall: 4 of 10 pre-registered hypotheses were supported; the other 6 are reported as not supported.
project.future_improvements:
• Collect questions from people living with both conditions, and get clinician review.
  • Add openly licensed sources that discuss the two conditions together.
  • Try multi-hop retrieval that joins one passage per condition.
  • Replace the keyword stage classifier with a small trained one, evaluated on new questions.
  • Calibrate the grounding checker on a larger human-labelled set, including list-style answers.
project.my_role:
I designed the project and led the build and evaluation end to end, working with an AI collaborator (Claude). The repository documents this split openly:

  • Mine: setting the research question and the starting design, and making the key decisions (choosing Render for the backend, running network steps on GitHub Actions). I also owned the pipeline, evaluation, website and deployment.
  • Written by the AI collaborator, as the repo states: the 148 evaluation questions, the gold labels, the stage-labelling rules and the hand audits. The README lists this as a circularity limitation.
project.key_learnings:
• That a strong semantic model plus a cross-encoder re-ranker can beat hand-built metadata logic, and that only a pre-registered test with paired intervals could show it.
  • How to build grounded generation: per-sentence citations, an abstention gate, and an independent NLI-based checker that doesn’t share a model with the answer writer.
  • Why evaluating the evaluator matters: the hand audit showed the automatic checker was conservative, which changes how its numbers should be read.
  • Designing safety layers for health information, and why rules tuned on development data aren’t evidence of performance on new questions.
  • Keeping an honest audit trail, including the circularity of having one AI collaborator write the questions, labels and audits.
  • Deploying ML under tight limits: ONNX quantization for a 512 MB server, checking that the live models match the evaluated ones, and an offline browser fallback.

related.title: Smart Resume Analyzer
related.short_description: An explainable resume job matching service that scores a resume against a job description using SBERT sentence embeddings, breaks the score down requirement by requirement, flags skill gaps and ATS formatting issues, and benchmarks its ranking quality on 8,000 labelled resume job pairs.
